A 64-year-old man presents with anaemia and blurring of vision with a haemoglobin level of 89 g/L. A total protein with a raised globulinfraction is noted.
A serum EPG shows an IgM paraprotein of 37 g/L. A bone marrow aspirate shows a lymphoplasmacytic inﬁltrate.
Which of the following would be the next most important investigation?
options: CT scan of head and orbits
explanation:
This man has a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma with an IgM paraprotein which is diagnostic of Waldenström macroglobulinaemia.
One of the serious complications of this condition is hyperviscosity syndrome. A plasma viscosity measurement would be essentialto diagnose and initiate treatment. The initial treatment would be plasmapheresis followed by cytoreductive therapy.
A skeletal survey, CT scan and PET scan are not particularly useful for diagnosis or prognosis of this condition.
A urine electrophoresis is a investigation that is necessary but not diagnostic in this situation where a diagnosis of hyperviscosityneeds to be made.
Reference:
García-Sanz R, Montoto S, Torrequebrada A, et al. Waldenström macroglobulinaemia: presenting features and outcome in a serieswith 217 cases. Br J Haematol. 2001;115:575-82.

A 30-year-old lady diagnosed with placenta praevia is noted to be bleeding from the site of cannulation during caesarean delivery.
Her laboratory investigations show a platelet count of 40 ×10/L, a ﬁbrinogen level of 0.4, prolonged PT at 14 seconds and an elevated
quantitative D-dimer.
What is the cornerstone of the treatment of DIC in this patient?
options: Anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin and anti-ﬁbrinolytic
explanation:
In 2009 the British Committee for Standards in Haematology (BCSH) released guidelines relating to the investigation andmanagement of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).
The cornerstone of the treatment of DIC is treatment of the underlying condition.
Transfusion of platelets or plasma components is reserved for patients who present with bleeding, and the diagnosis of DIC shouldencompass both laboratory and clinical ﬁndings. In this case, the underlying cause is the placenta praevia, and hence urgent deliveryof the fetus and removal of the inciting factor for the DIC (the placenta).
This of course should be supported by plasma and platelet transfusion; although all the blood product support options areappropriate, each one in isolation is not adequate to manage DIC.

A 37-year-old gentleman newly diagnosed with myeloma is commenced on treatment with dexamethasone and lenalidomide (animmunomodulatory drug in the same class of drugs as thalidomide).
Which treatment related issue MUST be discussed and clearly documented in the notes?
explanation:
Immunomodulatory drugs such as thalidomide and lenalidomide are now ﬁrst line medications in the treatment of myeloma. Themost common side effect of lenalidomide is myelosuppression, whereas somnolence, peripheral neuropathy and constipation areside effects of thalidomide.
The inherent, serious issue that is applicable to both medications is the teratogenic potential - all patients must be informed of thisrisk and advised regarding birth control and avoidance of sharing of medications with any other person.
It is not known whether lenalidomide is present in the semen of male patients receiving the drug. Therefore, males receivinglenalidomide must always use a latex condom during any sexual contact with females of childbearing potential even if they haveundergone a successful vasectomy.

A 70-year-old man presents with extensive ecchymoses and muscle bleeds. 
His APTT is prolonged at 41 seconds, and his platelet count and PT are within normal limits.  Plasma mixing studies do not correct theprolonged APTT, and a factor VIII inhibitor is detected.
What is the appropriate therapy in this case of acquired haemophilia A?
explanation:
This patient has an acquired Factor VIII inhibitor. Factor eight inhibitor bypassing agent (FEIBA) is a commercially available agentused in those with inhibitors and has a mix of several other activated clotting factors which bypass the factor VIII requiring step in thecoagulation pathway.
Acquired haemophilia is a rare disorder, with acquired allo-antibodies to factor VIII (rarely factor IX); it has known associations withunderlying malignancy and autoimmune conditions.
It is associated with a strong tendency towards bruising but with no or little joint bleeds. 
Management revolves around activated factor VII, with factor VIII not being eﬃcacious. 
Long term the inhibitor itself can be eradicated using immunosuppressants such as cyclophosphamide and corticosteroids.

She is asymptomatic apart from a few small neck nodes which her GP noticed on routine examination. Her full blood count, renal functionand LDH are normal.
Which of the following would be the next appropriate management plan?
explanation:
Asymptomatic patients with low grade lymphoma such as follicular lymphoma (grade 1 and 2) can be observed closely.
The value of intensive chemotherapy is questionable in asymptomatic patients. No long term survival beneﬁt has beendemonstrated with this approach.
An autologous or an allogeneic transplant would not be considered front line therapy for lymphomas.
Immunosuppressive therapy as a monotherapy is seldom employed as treatment in lymphomas.
Enrollment in a clinical trial would be an equally acceptable option in this case as best treatment approach is yet to be established. Ifthis patient were symptomatic or had end organ damage due to lymphoma she would have needed to start treatment.

He has no other sites of disease on staging and is systemically well.
Which of the following would be the ﬁrst line treatment of choice for this man?
options: Chemotherapy in combination with monoclonal antibodies
Triple therapy (proton pump inhibitor plus amoxicillin and clarithromycin)
explanation:
This man has Helicobacter pylori associated MALT lymphoma. The ﬁrst line therapy for this is using triple therapy (a commonregimen is a proton pump inhibitor, amoxicillin and clarithromycin). This usually results in resolution of the lymphoma in up to 80%of the cases.
Refractory or more widespread cases can be treated with systemic chemotherapy sometimes in combination with radiotherapy.
Monoclonal antibodies are now routinely used for treatment of B cell lymphomas but usually not as monotherapy.
Surgery is generally not a treatment option for lymphoma.

Which of the following is the cytogenetic abnormality seen in this lymphoma?
explanation:
This lady has a high grade lymphoma which is commonly referred to as Burkitt's lymphoma.
The characteristic cytogenetic abnormality is a reciprocal translocation t(8;14) while t( 11;14) (equivalent to cyclin D1) is seen inmantle cell lymphoma and t(14;18) is seen in cases of follicular lymphoma.
Burkitt's lymphoma is treated with intensive chemotherapy.  It has high response rates and is a haematological diagnosis which mustbe reached as an emergency in view of the high cell turnover.

An inpatient on the haematology ward develops a fever ﬁve minutes after starting a platelet transfusion. His temperature rises 1ºC from pre-transfusion observations.
Other than feeling hot he is well. His blood pressure, pulse and oxygen saturations are all unchanged from pre-transfusion observations. Anhour later he remains febrile, but is well and all other observations stable.
What is the most likely cause of his fever?
options: Leucocyte cytokines present in unit transfused
explanation:
With such a rapid rise in temperature one needs to consider a haemolytic transfusion reaction due to ABO incompatibility. However,several factors weigh against this as the diagnosis.
He is receiving a platelet transfusion, which does not typically contain the antigens necessary to provoke a transfusion reaction. It ispossible that the plasma in which the platelets are suspended contains a high titre of anti-A and anti-B antibodies, but this would beunusual. In addition, the clinical picture is not entirely consistent with ABO incompatibility: apart from a mild fever, the patient is verywell. With ABO incompatibility patients become shocked very quickly.
Febrile non-haemolytic reactions are very common, and are due to the presence of pyrogenic cytokines released from leucocytesduring storage of the platelet units. This is the most likely cause in this patient's case. The incidence is decreasing due toleucodepletion of blood products.
Bacterial contamination of platelets is common, due to the fact that they are stored at 22ºC. This supports growth; but thetemperature rise on transfusion is not usually as rapid.
Destruction of platelets by IgG is the process behind immune thrombocytopenia. Platelets are not usually transfused in thiscondition.
The history does not sound like an anaphylactoid reaction.

options: PET scan to rule out a malignancy
Bone marrow biopsy with Jak2 mutation status
Staging CT scan to rule out a lymphoma
Check iron status with investigation for occult blood loss
explanation:
Although a bone marrow biopsy or checking for bcr-abl mutation may be useful to conﬁrm a myeloproliferative disorder, ruling outiron deﬁciency as a cause for thrombocytosis is of paramount importance in this patient.
A gain of function somatic mutation of Janus kinase gene JAK2 V617F has been associated with myeloproliferative disorders. Thishas been decribed in >95% of patients with polycythaemia vera and in about 40-50% of patients with essential thrombocytosis.
A secondary cause for thrombocytosis is crucial to exclude before considering a diagnosis of a myeloproliferative disorder.
In fact, adequate iron stores are requisite diagnostic criteria (WHO) for essential thrombocytosis.
Imaging is not useful unless a speciﬁc pathology is being sought.

Which of the following clinical scenarios should lead the clinician to screen for thrombophilia?
options: Case ﬁnding in relatives of patient with unprovoked VTE
A 30-year-old female with deep vein thrombosis during ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome
explanation:
In 2009 the British Committee for Standards in Haematology (BCSH) released guidelines relating to the investigation of heritablethrombophilia.
Post-operative VTE is a provoked VTE and thus testing is not indicated.
Case ﬁndings of asymptomatic relatives with low risk thrombophilia such as factor V Leiden or the prothrombin gene mutation is notindicated.
There is no evidence for testing for thrombophilia in cases of cerebral or coronary thrombosis.
Purpura fulminans in children and neonates should lead one to test urgently for protein C and S deﬁciency.
Although ovarian hyperstimulation has been associated with an increased risk for thrombotic episodes, it is not an indication forthrombophilia testing.

explanation:

The diagnosis is one of exclusion, and in the absence of major bleeding, management would be observation, as it can resolvespontaneously.

You are asked to see a 55-year-old gentleman diagnosed with low risk myelodysplasia for the previous ﬁve years. He has been on atransfusion programme throughout and has received over 40 documented red cell concentrate transfusions.
His haemoglobin is stable in the 80-90 g/L range and the patient is asymptomatic. His ferritin is noted to be 2500 µg/L.
What is best course of action?
options: Repeated phlebotomy to get ferritin <500 µg/L
explanation:
Deposition of iron in secondary haemochromatosis (haemosiderosis) is detrimental to tissue function. Whereas phlebotomy iseffective at decreasing iron overload, in a patient who is anaemic this is not a viable option. Oral iron chelators, most notablydeferasirox, have revolutionized the treatment of this complication of repeated transfusions for chronic anaemia conditions.Desferrioxamine results in compliance issues due to the subcutaneous route and long infusion time, and deferiprone is considered asecond-line agent.
Deferiprone has been approved as second line in view of its side effect proﬁle, including bloody dyscrasias and liver dysfunction.Liver function tests are imperative whilst the patient is being administered both deferiprone and deferasirox.
Reference:
Aplastic Anaemia & MDS International Foundation. Iron Chelation Therapy.

She has stable renal function with a creatinine of 300 mmol/l and a creatinine clearance of 18 ml/min. Associated with her chronic renalfailure she has controlled secondary hyperparathyroidism. She has been anaemic for the last six months and investigation of dyspepsia withan OGD showed only mild gastritis. She has already been on oral ferrous sulphate 200 mg tds for three months.

A 34-year-old man with normal baseline cardiac and respiratory function starts on the ABVD (Adriamycin, Bleomycin, Vinblastine andDacarbazine) chemotherapy regimen for his stage IIB Hodgkin's lymphoma. He tolerated the ﬁrst three cycles of the chemotherapy well.
After completion of the 4th cycle, he presents with exertional dyspnoea and a dry cough. He is afebrile, a chest x ray and ECG are normal.
What is the most likely diagnostic possibility?
options: Hyperemesis and reﬂex cough related to dacarbazine
explanation:
Bleomycin related pulmonary ﬁbrosis is a major toxicity of the widely used ABVD regimen for treatment of Hodgkin's lymphoma. Ahigh resolution CT scan and pulmonary function tests are required to diagnose this condition. Oxygen therapy should be used withcaution in these patients as there is concern about further lung damage secondary to oxygen free radicals.
Although doxorubicin (also known as adriamycin) can cause cardiotoxicity, this is unusual at the doses used in this regimen and onewould expect abnormalities on the ECG.
He is afebrile, so Pneumocystis jirovecii is less likely though needs to be considered in the differential.
There is no history of hyperemesis given and a vinblastine neuropathy is unlikely to present as acute shortness of breath.

A 35-year-old lady diagnosed with iron deﬁciency anaemia has been extensively investigated, and with no source of blood loss ormalabsorption elucidated, has been commenced on oral iron supplementation with ferrous sulphate twice daily in view of a haemoglobin of75 g/L and ferritin of <5 µg/L.
Despite this, three months down the line, the iron indices and haemoglobin have failed to improve, and the patient reports bloating, loosebowel motions and nausea during consumption of the iron tablets, resulting in signiﬁcant loss of quality of life according to the patient.
What should be the next course of action?
options: Persist with same oral iron supplementation but alter dose
Change to other oral iron preparation
explanation:
Persisting with oral iron supplementation in view of the adverse events reported by the patient is a non-sequitur. Compliance is notan issue seeing the adverse events which are frequently associated with oral iron administration, although it can be veriﬁed byquerying the colour of the stool (black in iron administration).
Using red cell concentrate transfusion for a benign deﬁciency of iron is not appropriate. Parenteral (IV) iron is the proper course oftherapy, after discussion of risks involved (small risk of hypersensitivity).
Indications for IV iron include:Patients requiring iron supplementation who are unable to tolerate compounds given orally, orPatients with gastro-intestingal disorders, such as inﬂammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease), in whichsymptoms may be aggravated by oral iron therapy, orPatients who are unable to maintain acceptable iron levels during treatment with hemodialysisPatients who fail to comply with prescriptions for oral iron supplementation.
Reference:
Auerbach M, Ballard H. Clinical use of intravenous iron: administration, eﬃcacy, and safety. Hematology Am Soc Hematol EducProgram. 2010;2010:338-47.

A 52-year-old gentleman presents with:
Haemoglobin53 g/L (130-180)
WBC 250 ×10/L (4-11)
Platelet count25 ×10/L (150-400)
He is diagnosed with acute myeloid leukaemia and commenced on chemotherapy with daunorubicin and cytarabine. On day ﬁve the patientspikes a fever of 39°C, and has a tachycardia of 130 bpm and a blood pressure of 80/45 mmHg.
What is the most appropriate therapy at this point?
options: Fluid resucitation, blood and urine cultures followed by piperacillin/tazobactam + gentamicin
Blood and urine cultures followed by imipenem
explanation:
Febrile neutropenia in haematological malignancies is a medical emergency.
It is imperative that antimicrobials are commenced as soon as possible, if possible preceded by blood and urine cultures, but theemphasis should be on quick access to antimicrobials in appropriate doses and microbe cover.
Although the white cell count is elevated, functionally the patient is still neutropenic and the case should still be managed as febrileneutropenia.

Plasmapheresis is a treatment modality useful in a wide assortment of pathology involving harmful substances in the plasma which can beeﬃciently removed. Many conditions fall under this umbrella, including neurological, hematological, metabolic, and renal diseases, as well asintoxications, which can be effectively managed with plasma exchange.
In which of the following conditions is plasmapheresis considered as the ﬁrst-line standard of treatment?
explanation:
The American Society for Apheresis evaluates indications for apheresis and categorizes them from I to IV based on the availablemedical evidence for their use. Although plasmapheresis has a role in the management of AIHA, thyroid storm, ITP and SLE, its role ispoorly deﬁned, experimental and not evidence-based.
Other conditions where plasmapheresis is considered the ﬁrst line gold standard therapy include:myasthenia gravischronic inﬂammatory demyelinating polyneuropathyhyperviscosity in monoclonal gammopathiesthrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (using fresh frozen plasma)Goodpasture syndrome (unless dialysis dependent and no diffuse alveolar hemorrhage)haemolytic uremic syndrome (atypical form, due to autoantibody to factor H), andfulminant Wilson disease.
In most conditions 5% albumin is the plasma substitute of choice (to reduce the risk of pathogen transmission), except for TTPwhere it has a therapeutic role in replacing the missing factor, ADAMTS-13.

A 76-year-old retired steel industry employee is diagnosed with renal cell carcinoma.
It is noted that his full blood count is grossly abnormal:
Haemoglobin (Hb)203 g/L(130-180)
Haematocrit (PCV)0.60% (0.40-0.52)
Mean cell volume (MCV)90 fL (84-96)
White cell count (WBC)10 ×10/L (4.0-11.0)
Platelets 400 ×10/L (150-450)
Which of the following symptoms can be explained by the above blood test results?
explanation:
The above demonstrates a case of polycythaemia likely secondary to the renal cell carcinoma.
Polycythaemia can result in symptoms of the hyperviscosity syndrome, including:dizzinesstinnitusheadachesblurred vision, andpruritus.
A classic symptom of polycythemia vera is pruritus or itching, particularly after exposure to warm water (such as when taking a bath),which may be due to abnormal histamine release or prostaglandin production.

You see a 40-year-old male patient referred to the endocrinology clinic with newly diagnosed, poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, togetherwith lethargy and recent onset of erectile dysfunction.
The patient complains of bilateral knee discomfort and on examination is noted to have no discernible pathology except for 3 cmhepatomegaly. Blood investigations show deranged liver function tests.
What is the next course of action?
options: Genetic studies to assess for haemachromatosis genes
Serum ferritin and transferrin saturation calculation (fasting)
MRI to assess liver iron content
explanation:
Primary haemochromatosis is a genetic disorder resulting from a genetically determined predisposition to iron overload (type 1 to 4,including disorders of HFE, haemojuvelin, hepcidin, ferroportin or transferrin receptor-2 genes). It results in hepatic, endocrine,cardiac and dermatological manifestations. It is ideally diagnosed with fasting serum ferritin and transferrin saturation investigations,to be conﬁrmed by genetic studies for the varied genes known to be associated with primary haemochromatosis.
The reference range for men is 30-400 μ g/L, whilst for women this is 15‐150 μ g/L. Iron overload results in drastic elevations ofserum ferritin, usually >750 μ g/L, but other causes for elevated indices must be excluded and a fasting sample is preferred.
Reference:
British Society for Haematology. Genetic Haemochromatosis.

A 60-year-old lady presents to the Emergency Department at 1 am complaining of acute onset of headache, left upper and lower limbweakness, nausea, vomiting and lethargy.
Computed tomography of the head shows no intra-cranial pathology. Blood investigations show a haemoglobin of 60 g/L, a platelet count of5 × 10/L and mild renal impairment. Blood ﬁlm examination shows extensive red cell fragments and conﬁrms genuine thrombocytopenia.
What should be the immediate course of action?
options: Administer fresh frozen plasma till plasmapheresis is available
Proceed with plasmapheresis using fresh frozen plasma as plasma substitute
explanation:
The patient has severe thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), a pathology with high mortality rate unless recognizedimmediately and appropriate therapy instituted. TTP is classically described as a pentad of:MAHAthrombocytopenianeurological dysfunctionrenal impairment, andpyrexia.
However, all ﬁve are not usually present or required for diagnosis.
First line therapy is plasmapheresis with fresh frozen plasma as the plasma substitute (to replace the missing factor in TTP, calledADAMTS-13). Although fresh frozen plasma on its own and methylprednisolone, together with aspirin, are useful treatment optionsthey should in no way replace institution of plasmapheresis as soon as possible, except in centres where plasma exchange is notavailable 24/7.
Platelet transfusions are contra-indicated in TTP. The pathological basis relates to micro-thrombi formation which results inischaemia in affected blood vessels with ensuing end-organ damage (neurological, renal and cardiac).

A 25-year-old woman undergoing treatment for promyelocytic (M3) leukaemia develops a high fever.
Sepsis is suspected and she rapidly develops widespread ecchymoses and starts bleeding from venepuncture sites and mucous membranes.
Which is the most speciﬁc laboratory test to conﬁrm the diagnosis of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)?
options: D-dimer assay and ﬁbrin degradation products (FDP)
explanation:
The platelet count and the ﬁbrinogen level are almost always decreased in the presence of DIC.
Although these tests are not speciﬁc for DIC, normal levels exclude the possibility of DIC. The presence of schistocytes, or red cellfragments, is a frequent but non-speciﬁc ﬁnding in DIC.
Increased levels of FDPs occur in a variety of conditions in which clot formation and lysis occur.
D-dimers are produced by the action of plasmin on cross-linked ﬁbrin, not by the action of plasmin on unclotted ﬁbrinogen.
These tests reﬂect the microangiopathy of DIC and have been found to be sensitive, speciﬁc, and eﬃcient in the diagnosis of DIC.
In a recent review by Yu and colleagues, the combination of the D-dimer and the FDP assay provides the most rapid and speciﬁcdiagnosis of DIC.
References:1. Bick RL. Disseminated intravascular coagulation: pathophysiological mechanisms and manifestations. Semin Thromb Hemost.1998;24:3-18.2. Yu M, et al. Screening tests of disseminated intravascular coagulation: guidelines for rapid and speciﬁc laboratory diagnosis.Crit Care Med. 2000;28:1777-80.

A 68-year-old man with a lifelong history of recurrent epistaxis and intermittent haemoptysis presents for evaluation. He reports that hissymptoms began in his early twenties and that he has required occasional blood transfusions for anaemia. Lesions are shown below. 
What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) is an autosomal dominant vascular disorder characterised by abnormal dilated bloodvessels (telangiectasias) and arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) affecting the skin, mucous membranes, and internal organs.
Cutaneous and mucosal telangiectasias are typically seen on the face, lips, oral mucosa, and ﬁngertips.

A 35-year-old lady diagnosed with chronic kidney disease is found to be iron deﬁcient and is scheduled to commence intravenous ironcoupled with ESA (erythropoietin simulating agent). She has no prior history of hypersensitivity or anaphylaxis. She presents for her ﬁrstinfusion.
What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Proceed immediately with intravenous iron infusion
Administer a test dose, followed by remainder of infusion if no complications arise
explanation:
It is considered best practice to administer 1000 mg of low molecular weight iron dextran in 250 mL of normal saline in 1 hourwithout premedication; a test dose of 10 to 25 mg is infused over 3 to 5 minutes prior to the ﬁrst infusion. If no acute reaction isobserved, the remaining solution is infused over the balance of 1 hour. For those with a history of drug allergies or hypersensitivity,125 mg of methylprednisolone is infused prior to the test dose.
Although the safety of IV iron has been demonstrated in multiple studies, safety concerns still surround the issue of parenteral ironadministration. All iron products can cause hypersensitivity or anaphylaxis, some of which will be severe. The real incidence ofadverse events is not known, but one should consider avoiding high molecular weight iron dextran preparations based on publishedevidence up till now in the literature.
Reference:
Auerbach M, Ballard H. Clinical use of intravenous iron: administration, eﬃcacy, and safety. Hematology Am Soc Hematol EducProgram. 2010;2010:338-47.

A 39-year-old male ex-intravenous drug user (IVDU) presents to accident and emergency (A&E) with bloody diarrhoea and cramping pains inhis legs which have been worsening for a number of weeks. Six weeks ago he said he developed back pain which he attributes to gettingolder but this has not improved. The patient is known to have intermittent claudication and a recent Ankle Brachial Pressure Index (ABPI) is inkeeping with severe disease.
A full body CT angiogram is performed which shows emboli in the leg and some in the mesentery, with a larger mass in the ascending aorta.
On examination, the patient has an ejection systolic murmur heard loudest at the right heart border 2nd heart border.
Observations are stable and the patient is apyrexial.
What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
options: Embolic events secondary to intra-aortic thrombus
Massive Pulmonary embolus (PE) with secondary emboli
explanation:
This may seem a fairly straightforward question at ﬁrst but this could be a number of diagnoses. Aortic valve endocarditis is high upon the list of differentials but in the absence of pyrexia and the fact that the patient is reported to be an ex-IVDU make this less likely.
Mesenteric ischaemia would be highly likely given the presentation but the subsequent imaging makes this unlikely as theunderlying primary pathology.
A fat embolus is more common in long bone fractures and would present with skin changes.
Massive PE is also another possibility but is once again unlikely given the conclusive imaging. This makes an embolic eventsecondary to intra- aortic thrombus the most likely diagnosis. Years of damage following intravenous drug abuse could result inatherosclerosis and high susceptibility to thrombus formation. 
Further reading:
Large Free-Floating Intra-Aortic Thrombus

A 65-year-old man was diagnosed with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia.
What antimicrobial prophylaxis should he receive before starting chemotherapy with ﬂudarabine?
explanation:
Fludarabine is a purine analogue that is phosphorylated intracellularly.
All of the purine analogues cause myelosuppression, but there is a signiﬁcantly higher risk of patients developing Pneumocystisjirovecii pneumonia while on treatment.
Use of prophylactic co-trimoxazole (Septrin) has dramatically reduced the frequency of this severe opportunistic infection in thesepatients.
Co-trimoxazole should be continued after chemotherapy until the CD4 counts exceeds 200 cells/mm (0.2 ×10/L).

A 32-year-old lady, 40 days post matched unrelated donor (MUD) allogeneic bone marrow transplant in her second remission of her acutemyeloid leukaemia complains of loose bowel motions and a maculopapular rash over her extremities.
Her liver function tests showed an elevated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, with sparing of ALT and GGT. The patient is diagnosed with acutegraft versus host disease.
What is the most appropriate initial management?
explanation:
Acute graft versus host is the major cause of early transplant-related morbidity and mortality. It is characterised by fever, rash,abnormal LFTs, diarrhoea, suppression of engraftment and viral reactivation.
Management revolves around good nutrition, weight maintenance and immunosuppression with methylprednisone andcyclosporin.
Tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil are second line agents for the use of acute GvHD.

A 10-year-old boy is noticed to be jaundiced on return from a holiday in Africa with his parents. He is on antimalarial prophylaxis.
His complete blood count shows haemoglobin of 80 g/L, with Heinz bodies and blister cells on blood ﬁlm examination.
Which of the following relates to this disorder?
options: Transfusion is strictly merited in each case
The antimalarial prophylaxis has no relation to the laboratory ﬁndings
This is a common autosomal dominant disorder
It is most commonly precipitated by peas
Treatment involves strict avoidance of known precipitants
explanation:
This question relates to the management of G-6-PD deﬁciency.
G-6-PD is the most common inherited enzyme defect in humans; an X linked inheritance pattern.
It is mostly commonly precipitated by several classes of drugs, including antimalarials and is also associated with ingestion of broadbeans (favism).
Treatment revolves around avoidance of all known precipitating factors, and blood product support should only be given in unstable,symptomatic patients.

This peripheral blood smear is obtained on a 16-year-old female with Down syndrome who is admitted with abdominal cramps andconstipation:
Investigations reveal:
Haemoglobin98 g/L (115-165)
Platelet count210 ×10/L (150-400)
White cell count5.5 ×10/L (4-11)
Which of the following would account for her presentation and appearance of the blood ﬁlm?
explanation:
The blood ﬁlm shows basophilic (blue) stippling of the red cells which is typical of lead poisoning.
This occurs due to accumulation of ribonucleic acid (RNA) in the red blood cells due to inhibition of pyrimidine 5 nucleotidase bylead. The denatured RNA is revealed as basophilic stippling.
Other features include mild anaemia, encephalopathy and peripheral motor neuronopathies.
Patients with learning disabilities may be prone to lead poisoning due to pica.

A 21-year-old lady diagnosed with severe type 1 von Willebrand disease is planned to undergo emergency appendicectomy. 
After informing the coagulation laboratory that monitoring will be required with vWF:RCo or vWF:Ag, which coagulation factor is the mostappropriate for the management of this patient with von Willebrand disease?
explanation:
von Willebrand disease is the commonest heritable bleeding disorder.
Type 1 vWD is responsible for 75% of the cases of vWD and is related to quantitative deﬁciency of vWD. 
For treatment of acute bleeding or emergency surgery, a VWF‐FVIII concentrate or a combination of high purity FVIII and high purityVWF concentrates should be used as per the British Society of Haematology guidelines. In patients with severe bleeding orundergoing surgical procedures where any increase in bleeding carries risk, such as a neurosurgical procedure and/or whensustained levels of von Willebrand factor (VWF) are needed for several days, a VWF-containing concentrate should be used.
Most VWF concentrates contain both VWF and factor VIII. However, in patients given high-purity VWF, it takes approximately 6-8hours for the endogenous levels of factor VIII to reach haemostatic levels.  Therefore, an initial loading dose of factor VIII must begiven when bleeding is treated with high-purity plasma VWF concentrate or recombinant VWF concentrate.

A 33-year-old male develops a rash and low grade fever (37.6°C) 21 days post allogeneic bone marrow transplant for high risk acute myeloidleukaemia in ﬁrst complete remission.
The rash is initially maculopapular affecting palms and soles but 24 hours later general erythroderma is noted affecting the trunk and limbs.His total bilirubin was previously normal but is now noted to be 40 µmol/L (1-22). He remains very well in himself.
What would be your management of this patient at this stage?
explanation:
This is classical graft versus host disease post bone marrow transplant.
Acute graft versus host disease (GVHD) occurs in the ﬁrst 100 days post transplant with chronic GVHD occurring 100-300 days posttransplant.
GVHD is graded according to the Seattle system, and each organ involved is scored (skin, liver and gut). So this patient has twosystems involved.
The candidate should ﬁrst recognise that this is the diagnosis and should also know that observation is not an option for GVHD.
The standard initial treatment in the acute setting is high dose methylprednisolone. Action is needed quickly. If there is no responsethen more intensive immunosuppression is needed such as Campath or antilymphocyte globulin.
Oral prednisolone is the choice for chronic GVHD.

A 26-year-old man attends the dental hospital for a tooth extraction.
He reports prolonged bleeding after a tooth extraction two years previously. He has had no other surgical challenges and no other history ofprolonged bleeding. He is otherwise ﬁt and well.
On further questioning he said his mother had recently been referred to a local hospital for recurrent nose bleeds and menorrhagia. He wasalso aware that his sister had been seen in the past for menorrhagia.
The dental extraction cannot be delayed.
What should the dentist be advised to give the patient to reduce the risk of signiﬁcant bleeding?
explanation:
The bleeding described is a defect of primary haemostasis. It is inherited as mother and sister are affected.
The most likely diagnosis is von Willebrand (vWB) disease. It is likely to be mild (type I) as the patient and family members havereached a good age with no major bleeding problems.
The most appropriate management is therefore good surgical technique, pressure and oral tranexamic acid. The side effects areminimal.
The choice of treatment for a mild vWB facing a more invasive procedure would be DDAVP, providing there is no contraindication.vWB factor concentrate would be reserved as second line treatment to DDAVP.
FFP and cryoprecipitate are not used in von Willebrand disease.
Haemophilia is not the diagnosis with a defect of primary haemostasis and generally females are not affected as it is X linked.

A 55-year-old man was referred to the outpatient clinic with anaemia.
He had presented to his general practitioner with a three month history of fatigue and low back pain. There was no preceding history oftrauma. A plain x ray of his lumbar spine showed a lytic lesion in the body of the fourth lumbar vertebra (L4).
Investigations revealed:
Haemoglobin 105 g/L(130-180)
WBC 4.0 ×10/L (4-11)
Platelets 175 ×10/L (150-400)
Serum sodium137 mmol/L(137-144)
Serum potassium3.5 mmol/L(3.5-4.9)
Serum urea 2.7 mmol/L(2.5-7.5)
Serum creatinine110 µmol/L(60-110)
Serum corrected calcium2.4 mmol/L(2.2-2.6)
Bence Jones proteins were detected in the urine.
A skeletal survey showed increased uptake in the L4.
Which of the following therapies will reduce the risk of pathological fracture?

A 60-year-old lady with a history of diabetes mellitus, essential hypertension and ischaemic heart disease with a myocardial infarct, is notedto have platelet count of 700 × 10/L (150-400).
Bone marrow biopsy shows increased megakaryocytes with lobulated nuclei and abnormal localisation. JAK-2 mutation is positive.
What is the correct management of this patient with essential thrombocythaemia?
explanation:
Essential thrombocythaemia is a clonal myeloproliferative disorder characterised by an elevated platelet count in the absence of areactive cause for the thrombocytosis.
Fifty per cent of cases are positive for the JAK-2 mutation. Positivity for JAK-2 mutation, a platelet count above 600 × 10/L and apast history of thrombosis entail a higher risk, especially in the presence of other vascular risk factors such as hypertension, diabetesmellitus, ischaemic heart disease and/or peripheral vascular disease.
The management is based on cytoreduction with hydroxycarbamide and an antiplatelet agent such as aspirin to decrease thethrombotic risk.
Anagrelide is a second line drug in ET and has been associated with increased bone marrow ﬁbrosis.
Interferon has a use in ET in the setting of pregnancy.

stem:
The anticoagulation nurse phones you for advice.
A 73-year-old lady is on warfarin for atrial ﬁbrillation, her normal INR range falls between 2.0-3.0. She has recently been started onclarithromycin for a chest infection; her INR has now come back at greater than 9.0.
What should you advise?
options: Stop warfarin and administer vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma (FFP)
Stop warfarin, administer vitamin K, re-start warfarin when INR less than 5
Stop warfarin, stop clarithromycin and seek haematology advice
Stop warfarin and convert to IV heparin (high risk of stroke)
explanation:
As per British Journal of Haematology (BJH) guidelines:
INR >8.0, no bleeding or minor bleeding:Stop warfarin and give phytomenadione (vitamin K) 2.5-5 mg by mouth using the intravenous preparation orally (unlicensed
use), or 0.5-1 mg by slow intravenous injection (if complete reversal required 5-10 mg by slow intravenous injection); repeatdose of phytomenadione if INR still too high after 24 hours; restart warfarin when INR <5.0.

The mass has appeared rapidly and this would make you think of a lymphoproliferative disorder with a short doubling time, forexample, Burkitt's lymphoma. The clue to this is that he is from Africa, with Burkitt's being endemic in parts of Africa, and can also beseen with immunodeﬁciency states such as HIV.
Only a lymph node biopsy will give you a deﬁnitive diagnosis.
A bone marrow and full body CT is done as part of staging a lymphoproliferative disorder, but will not necessarily provide you with adeﬁnitive diagnosis.

There were widespread petechiae on the limbs. Her respiratory rate was measured at 28 breaths per minute. Her heart sounds were normaland the chest clear. Her abdomen was soft, but she was very tender in the suprapubic region and a mass was felt rising from the pelvic brim.
After taking blood, it was noted that there was continued bleeding from the venous puncture site. A urinary catheter was inserted andyielded 1500 ml of cloudy yellow offensive-smelling urine.

A 58-year-old female presents with a platelet count of 768 ×10/L (150 - 400).
On examination she has isolated mild splenomegaly. The history and remainder of the examination are non-contributory.
What would be the next most useful diagnostic test?
options: Bone marrow biopsy with molecular studies
explanation:
The presence of splenomegaly in the setting of a raised platelet count suggests a diagnosis of a myeloproliferative disorder.
A bone marrow biopsy with ancillary studies would be useful in the diagnosis.
Although not speciﬁc for any myeloproliferative disorder, mutations of the Janus kinase 2 region are found in the majority ofpolycythaemia vera and in a signiﬁcant proportion of essential thrombocytosis. There are also certain morphological features in themegakaryocytes on the bone marrow trephine which would be useful along with assessment of marrow iron stores. Hence bonemarrow biopsy with molecular studies would be the next most useful diagnostic test.
Radiology is not particularly useful and ﬂow cytometry ﬁndings are usually not speciﬁc in these disorders. Splenic biopsy is usuallynot undertaken for diagnosis of myeloproliferative disorders.

A 32-year-old female suffers multiple traumas in a road traﬃc accident including fracture of her pelvis, right femur and left humerus. She istaken immediately to theatre for surgery.
During surgery and immediately post operatively she has extensive life threatening bleeding and requires 24 units of red cells, 6 units ofplatelets and 16 units of fresh frozen plasma. She undergoes a stormy post operative recovery initially on the intensive care unit and thenthe general ward.
You are called to see her ﬁve days post operatively. She is receiving a blood transfusion and has spiked a temperature 45 minutes afterstarting a unit of red cells. Her temperature is 38.2°C and blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg and heart rate is 98 bpm. The red cell transfusionis stopped and patient identity checked and the unit of blood is checked against her identity, all appear to be correct.
A transfusion reaction investigation is initiated by the hospital's transfusion practitioner and transfusion team. The patient is monitoredclosely and remains well over the next 24 hours. Her temperature returned to normal within 20 minutes of stopping the transfusion.
Further information emerges the next day following investigations. The patient is blood group A rhesus D negative, and the unit of bloodbeing transfused during the above reported reaction was of the correct group and cross match compatible. However, it appears that duringher emergency surgery and subsequent bleeding she received 2 units of rhesus D positive platelets.
What action do you advise now?
options: Measure anti D titre in patient
Advise that this is of no further consequence to her
Advise patient that this is only likely to be of consequence should she become pregnant in the future.
explanation:
The transfusion reaction described is likely to be a febrile transfusion reaction. Following the investigations there does not appear tobe an ABO incompatible transfusion. Her temperature settles after stopping the transfusion and she is not that unwell.
Febrile transfusion reactions are common and are due to anti HLA antibodies in recipient serum or granulocyte speciﬁc antibodies(for example, sensitisation during previous pregnancy or previous blood transfusion).
All hospitals have (or should have) a transfusion team and committee to report, amongst other things, transfusion related eventsand reactions to SHOT (serious hazards of transfusion) and SABRE (serious adverse blood related events).

options: Transfusion of two units group O rhesus D negative blood
explanation:
The clinical picture is disseminated intravascular coagulation.
When bleeding is the major problem, the aim is to maintain the prothrombin and activated thromboplastin time at a ratio of 1.5times of the control and the ﬁbrinogen level above 1 g/L.
Platelet transfusion is recommended if the count is less than 50 ×10/L.
Anaemia is not very severe so in this case ﬁbrinogen replacement would be the appropriate ﬁrst choice with blood transfusion anaddition if bleeding continues and patient develops hypovolaemic shock.

Which of the following is true about thrombophilia testing?
options: This patient warrants testing as he is less than 60 years of age

The most common known heritable thrombophilia is prothrombin gene mutation
A thrombosis in an unusual vascular territory warrants thrombophilia testing
Patients with provoked DVT should always be tested for thrombophilia
explanation:
Thrombophilia testing is considered useful in patients presenting with:A ﬁrst episode of venous thromboembolism (VTE) at a young age (usually considered less than 45 years of age)Idiopathic venous thrombosis (this patient clearly has a provoked DVT relating to a fracture)A family history of thrombosis, particularly in a ﬁrst degree relativeVTE in an unusual vascular territoryNeonatal purpura fulminansWarfarin induced skin necrosis
Factor V Leiden is the commonest heritable thrombophilia, a heterozygote state is seen in about 5% of the general Caucasianpopulation.

Her blood count shows a WBC of 6.3 ×10/L (normal diff), haemoglobin of 115 g/L, and a platelet count of 3 ×10/L.
What would be the most appropriate next treatment modality provided the presence of accessory spleens having been excluded?
options: All of the above are acceptable; treatment should be patient-centred as regards choice of immunosuppressive agent
explanation:
The management of immune thrombocytopenic purpura post-splenectomy is based around exclusion of accessory splenic tissue byimaging studies and conﬁrming post-splenectomy changes (Howell-Jolly bodies and target cells) on blood ﬁlm examination.
There is a move towards thrombopoietin agonists even in this setting but there is no evidence for their use in this setting.Thrombopoietin agonists are expensive and the durability of the response is directly proportional to their administration, withplatelets decreasing again in most cases when the thrombopoietin agonist is discontinued.
In such a situation post-splenectomy all of the immunosuppressants mentioned above are valid options and the decision aboutwhich drug to use should be discussed with the patient and on a case by case basis.

Her blood results come back with:

The patient is diagnosed with suspected thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and transferred to ITU.

explanation:
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is a rare disorder characterised by increased platelet aggregation due to abnormaldeposition of vWF multimers.
Mortality is 90% unless diagnosed and treated urgently, falling to 10% if treated appropriately. The most appropriate treatment isplasmapheresis with fresh frozen plasma, although fresh frozen plasma transfusion alone is useful as a holding measure till access toplasmapheresis is established.
Platelet transfusion is actually deleterious and should not be administered.
Aspirin and cyclosporin are useful only in the management of chronic TTP to decrease the chance of relapse.

explanation:
The most appropriate product is recombinant factor VIII since it results in the least exposure of the patient to transmissibleinfections and human donors. Thus recombinant factor VIII is the most appropriate answer.
Cryoprecipitate has no use in haemophilia A and plasma derived factor VIII is used only where there is no access to recombinantfactor VIII.
FEIBA and NovoSeven are of use in the management of haemophilia patients who have developed a high titre inhibitor, which in thiscase is not present.

explanation:

On examination she appeared well. She was afebrile. Xanthelasma were noted around both eyes. A few faint scratch marks were visible onthe skin of her arms. She attributed this to an 'allergy' to a new washing powder.

Over 90% of cases of primary biliary cirrhosis (PBC) occur in women aged 35 to 70.
The presentation is usually insidious. Pruritus, non-speciﬁc fatigue, or both are the initial symptoms in more than 50% of patientsand can precede other symptoms by months or years.
About 50% of patients present with an enlarged, ﬁrm, non-tender liver; 25%, with splenomegaly; about 15%, with skin xanthomas;and 10%, with hyperpigmentation.

There are no speciﬁc red cell morphology features
It is caused by vertical red cell membrane, that is, ankyrin spectrin link defect
The red cells haemolyse on exposure to drugs
explanation:
Red cell membrane defects are broadly classiﬁed into hereditary spherocytosis (HS), hereditary elliptocytosis (HE) and others.
Horizontal membrane protein defects (for example, spectrin ankyrin interaction defect) results in HE whereas vertical defects resultin hereditary spherocytosis.
Elliptocytosis is usually caused by spectrin and spectrin-protein 4.1 defects.
Heterozygotes are asymptomatic but show elliptocytes on blood ﬁlm; they do not have haemolysis and do not require any particulartreatment (hence excluding other options).

A 32-year-old man presents to the pre-assessment clinic prior to lumbar spine surgery. He tells you he has recently been diagnosed withtype 1 von Willebrand disease following an episode of bleeding after minor surgery.
In discussion with the haematologists you arrange crossmatched blood and platelets to be available on the day of the surgery.
Which of the following haematological products should be administered prior to surgery?
explanation:
Type 1 von Willebrand disease patients have up to a 50% reduction in von Willebrand factor (vWF). Many are asymptomatic and areonly diagnosed following an episode of bleeding associated with a dental extraction or minor surgery.
In minor trauma, desmopressin (DDAVP) can be used to increase the concentration of VWF. However for major surgery, factor VIIIconcentrate is used to increase the concentration of vWF. The most commonly used is Humate-P.
Puriﬁed or recombinant preparations are avoided since they contain only small concentrations of vWF.
Further Reading:
Ridley S, Taylor B, Gunning K. Medical management of bleeding in critically ill patients. Contin Educ Anaesth Crit Care Pain.2007;7:116-121.

review.

options: CT scan of chest abdomen and pelvis
Presence of smear cells on the blood ﬁlm
explanation:
Flow cytometry showing a speciﬁc pattern of monoclonal B cell proliferation (CD19/5 co expressing, CD23 positive, light chainrestricted B cell population) is diagnostic of CLL.
CT scan and LDH are investigations needed to complete staging but not essential for diagnosis. Smear cells are reported in otherlymphoproliferative as well as benign lymphocytosis and merely indicate fragile lymphocytes which are artefactually smeared on theglass slide.
Cervical lymphadenopathy may be seen in CLL but can also be seen in any other cause of lymphadenopathy (e.g. viral infections,adenopathy secondary to local dental infection).

On further enquiry the lady gives a history of her mother having a splenectomy for her anaemia.
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Hereditary elliptocytosis (HE) heterozygote is usually asymptomatic without haemolysis.
Thalassaemia and sickle cell anaemia can cause gallstones but often have speciﬁc blood ﬁlm changes. For example, microcytichypochromic red cells in thalassaemia and sickle cells in sickle cell anaemia respectively.
Autoimmune haemolysis would show a positive DAT.
The history of anaemia in the family, with numerous spherocytes and a negative DAT, suggests hereditary spherocytosis as thecause of anaemia in this case.
A history of neonatal jaundice should also be sought.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This young man has a pancytopenia with a hypocellular marrow therefore the diagnosis is most likely aplastic anaemia.
Leukaemias are generally hypercellular and myelodysplastic syndrome is unusual in this age group (but not unheard of, especially ifthere is a previous history of ionising radiation or alkylating agent use). Therefore the answer is not acute lymphoblastic, acutemyeloid leukaemia or myelodysplastic syndrome.
Haemolytic anaemias may cause pancytopenia in the setting of hypersplenism, paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH) oraplastic crisis (due to erythrovirus infection) but there are usually other clues or indicators in those circumstances. Hence the answeris not haemolytic anaemia.

Which parameter is most useful to decide whether this patient requires active treatment?
options: The presence or absence of bleeding
explanation:
In 2009 the British Committee for Standards in Haematology (BCSH) released guidelines relating to the diagnosis and managementof disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).
Transfusion of platelets or plasma components in patients with DIC should not be primarily based on laboratory results and should ingeneral be reserved for patients who present with bleeding. Hence the most useful parameter for deciding whether this patientrequires active treatment would be the presence or absence of bleeding.
